text: Core CS for SWE Hiring in India Executive summary For general SWE/SDE hiring in India, Data Structures and Algorithms remains the single biggest gatekeeper, especially at the online assessment, phone-screen, and coding-round stages across Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Flipkart, Swiggy, and startup/product-company loops. Official interview-prep material from Amazon, Microsoft, and Flipkart all foreground coding, algorithms, problem solving, object-oriented design, and design/system thinking; recent candidate reports from India and India-targeted teams show the same pattern. Operating Systems matters, but usually as a tier-two subject rather than the first gate for mainstream SWE roles. In most entry-level and early-career generalist hiring, OS is rarely the decisive factor in resume screening or coding OAs. Its value shows up later: technical interviews, project deep dives, machine-coding/ OOD rounds, and system-design or backend/platform discussions. OS becomes much more important for backend/platform/infrastructure/support roles, and for teams that explicitly mention distributed systems, performance, scalability, or production operations. Amazon’s India-linked job postings explicitly call out OS, OOD, algorithms, and data structures; Flipkart’s own prep guide says OS basics are essential for system design; Microsoft emphasizes distributed systems and design; startup/product roles in India increasingly ask for large-scale distributed systems experience. The practical ranking for most candidates with a CS background targeting general SWE/SDE roles in India is: DSA OOP/OOD DBMS + SQL Operating Systems Computer Networks System Design Concurrency / Multithreading SDLC / testing / debugging / project depth Compilers for specialized roles only That ranking changes for mid-level backend/platform roles: system design and distributed systems jump near the top, and OS/networking/concurrency become more important because they are embedded inside design, performance, and debugging discussions. Google candidate reports from India show L4/L5 loops that are heavily DSA-driven but include system design depending on level and interview structure; Microsoft’s official guidance similarly weights design and distributed systems strongly for applicable roles. For Indian IT-services fresher roles such as TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, the picture is different. text: technical interviews rather than dominating the entire process. Recent TCS/Infosys/Wipro process summaries show TCS NQT centered on aptitude and coding, Infosys assessment emphasizing reasoning, pseudocode, English, and puzzle/problem sections, and Wipro combining aptitude, coding, and a lighter technical interview that often asks OS, DBMS, and OOP basics rather than deep system design. From a time-efficiency perspective, the best fast-learning stack for a CS student is: NeetCode or Striver for DSA, OSTEP selected chapters for OS, SQLBolt plus selective DB lectures for DBMS, a selective networking course for CN, Refactoring.Guru for OOD/design patterns, and structured mock/problem practice. For most India-focused interview prep, an 8-week plan is the best tradeoff between speed and retention; a 4-week plan works only if you restrict scope to the minimum interview-relevant topics and practice aggressively. Market context and method India’s software hiring market in 2025–2026 has been selective rather than uniformly weak. TeamLease EdTech reported that 70% of employers intended to hire freshers in July–December 2025, with e- commerce and technology startups at 88% and Bangalore leading major cities at 81%. The same report describes a shift toward job-ready, digitally skilled freshers rather than purely volume hiring. Naukri’s 2026 JobSpeak summaries show white-collar hiring growth with AI/ML demand notably stronger than general IT, while Reuters and GCC-focused reporting indicate continued expansion of global capability centers and multinational engineering presence in India. That market context matters because it changes what gets screened. In a precision-hiring environment, companies are not usually testing “academic completeness”; they are testing whether you can clear the specific bottleneck of their process. For TCS/Infosys/Wipro, that bottleneck is often the assessment plus communication. For Amazon/Google/Microsoft and top Indian product companies, it is still typically coding/ problem solving first, then design/project depth. Official company guidance strongly supports that interpretation. Amazon’s university and SDE interview pages emphasize coding, algorithms, OOD, databases, distributed computing, OS, and system design; Microsoft’s official guidance evaluates problem solving, design, coding, testing, and—in relevant roles—distributed systems; Flipkart’s own guide separates problem-solving/data-structure and design rounds and explicitly recommends brushing up OOP, design patterns, system architecture, distributed systems, Internet basics, and OS basics. This report uses four evidence buckets from roughly the last two to three years: official interview-prep pages and job postings, recent candidate experiences from LeetCode/Medium/GeeksforGeeks, recruiter/career guidance from company career pages, and India hiring reports. Where public company-specific evidence was sparse, I grouped firms into clusters instead of pretending there is a precise company-by-company scoring rubric. In particular, Ola and several smaller startups had limited recent accessible public process evidence, so they are treated inside an Indian product/startup cluster rather than given a false precision score. The weight tables below are therefore analytical estimates, not official hiring rubrics. A second methodological point: resume screening is not very “subject-driven” in the same way coding rounds are. Resumes are screened more through signals like internships, known brands, project depth, open-source work, contest/problem-solving profiles, and stack fit. Microsoft officially evaluates problem solving, design, coding, testing, and says distributed systems knowledge is very important where relevant. Google job postings still foreground DSA and software design, while Google candidate reports from India show DSA- dominant loops with system design added depending on level/packet. Bottom line on OS For general SWE roles, OS is usually not more important than DSA, OOP/OOD, DBMS, or system design. But it is still important enough that skipping it entirely is a mistake. A good rule of thumb is: TCS / Infosys / Wipro general fresher roles: OS is moderately useful, mostly for technical interviews, and rarely a first-stage gate. Amazon / Microsoft / Google general SWE: OS is secondary but real; it helps in team-fit, project deep dive, technical follow-ups, and any systems-oriented discussion. Flipkart / Swiggy / startups / backend-platform roles: OS is more important than many students assume, because it appears disguised inside queues, caches, concurrency, latency, retries, locking, resource contention, and machine-coding design. Compiler / kernel / infra / networking / systems roles: OS can become top-tier, and compilers/ networking can also jump from low-priority to critical. Google’s TPU Compiler role is an example of a specialist posting where compiler- and systems-oriented depth matters far more than for mainstream SWE roles. How important OS and core CS really are The simplest defensible answer is this: OS is not the main gate; it is the multiplier. DSA gets you through the door because it dominates OAs, live coding, and early technical filtering. That is overwhelmingly clear from Amazon’s official OA structure, Microsoft’s coding-first advice, Flipkart’s PS/DS round, and recent Amazon/Google/Microsoft/Flipkart/Swiggy reports. OS then acts as a multiplier in three situations. 14 • 15 • 16 • 17 • 18 19 6

text: First, it helps when you are asked to reason about real production behavior: why a service slows down, why threads deadlock, why performance tanks under contention, how memory pressure changes behavior, why a file write is not durable immediately, or why containerized systems differ from full VMs. This is why official prep material from Flipkart and Amazon connects OS to design and systems discussions, not just textbook viva questions. Second, it strengthens machine coding and OOD. Many companies do not ask “Explain page replacement” in isolation; instead they ask for a design—parking lot, Splitwise, chess game, notification platform, distributed cache—and then evaluate whether you understand thread safety, state, resource ownership, lifecycle, and failure modes. Recent Amazon fresher and Microsoft practice accounts show exactly this combination of DSA plus machine-coding/OOD/constraint-follow-ups. Third, OS becomes valuable in project deep dives and HM rounds because interviewers trust evidence of applied understanding more than memorized definitions. Flipkart’s phone screen and exploratory stage, Microsoft’s official guidance, and Google candidate reports all make clear that interviewers probe your prior projects and technical choices. If your résumé contains backend, systems, cloud, databases, web servers, compilers, or any performance-sensitive system, OS knowledge becomes part of how believable your project explanations sound. For a student or early-career engineer with limited time, the implication is very practical: learn OS to interview depth, not to full-academic depth. That means understanding the concepts and being able to apply them in explanations, trade-offs, and simple design/problem contexts. You do not need a full graduate-level systems course for most interview loops. You do need enough depth to answer confidently and connect OS ideas to code and architecture. text: The evidence base is unusually consistent here. Flipkart explicitly names DSA, OOD, design patterns, system architecture, CAP, distributed systems, and OS/Internet basics. Amazon lists DSA, OOD, databases, distributed computing, and OS. Microsoft’s official guidance adds testing and distributed systems. Recent technical experiences from Microsoft, TCS, Wipro, and Infosys show DBMS, OOP, OS, and SDLC/Agile concepts appearing most often as supporting technical knowledge, not as the central first-round gate. Fastest interview-resilient OS coverage If your goal is interview efficiency, prioritize this OS subset: processes vs threads context switching scheduling basics synchronization primitives deadlocks and starvation virtual memory, paging, TLB, page faults heap vs stack, fragmentation file-system basics and durability intuition VM vs container one or two real examples of concurrency bugs in your own code That subset covers the majority of OS-style questions you are likely to face in general SWE/SDE interviews in India. It also maps well into design reasoning for backend, platform, or machine-coding rounds. Study plans and minimal checklists Recommended time budgets Assuming you already have basic CS exposure: 4-week crash plan: about 3–4 hours/day on weekdays, 5–6 hours/day on weekends 8-week balanced plan: about 2–3 hours/day on weekdays, 4–5 hours/day on weekends 12-week strong plan: about 1.5–2.5 hours/day consistently The 4-week option is enough to become interview-viable for many entry-level loops. The 8-week option is the best default if you want to cover DSA plus enough OS/DBMS/CN/OOD to sound credible in technical discussions. The 12-week option is the best choice if you are targeting product companies, startups, or 2+ YOE backend/platform roles where system design is likely. This recommendation follows directly from the relative interview weight of DSA first, then OOD/design, then core-CS support topics. 25 • • • • • • • • • • 26 • • • 27 9

text: Timeline visual The plan structure mirrors what current India hiring loops actually reward: DSA first, then OOD/design, then core-CS reinforcement, then mock execution. Four-week crash plan Week one Focus almost entirely on DSA foundations and SQL basics. Finish arrays, strings, hashing, sliding window, two pointers, stack/queue, and binary search. Add 30–45 minutes per day of SQL or DBMS basics so that joins, group by, normalization, and ACID do not feel foreign. The goal is to make yourself OA-ready immediately. This is the highest-return week because OAs and first technical rounds are still overwhelmingly DSA-heavy. Week two Cover trees, heaps, graphs, BFS/DFS, and basic dynamic programming. Start OS with processes vs threads, scheduling, synchronization, deadlocks, and virtual memory basics. At the end of the week, do one mock technical round with a friend or by recording yourself. This is where you convert from “practice mode” to “interview mode.” Week three Finish DBMS essentials, networking basics, and OOP/OOD essentials. Learn SOLID, common design patterns, class modeling, and one or two machine-coding classics such as Splitwise, parking lot, chess, or elevator. This maps directly to Flipkart-style design/OOD rounds and the machine-coding/OOD flavor that increasingly appears in Amazon/startup/product loops. Week four Run mixed interview simulations: two coding rounds, one OOD/machine-coding discussion, one system- design-lite round, one behavioral/project deep dive. Review your resume line by line and prepare stories for each project, especially anything involving databases, web servers, APIs, concurrency, or scaling. Companies repeatedly probe project depth and role fit at the later stages. text: [ ] Be comfortable with arrays, strings, hash maps, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, heaps, binary search, DFS/BFS, basic DP [ ] Learn joins, normalization, ACID, indexes, transactions [ ] Learn processes/threads, deadlocks, synchronization, virtual memory [ ] Learn HTTP, TCP basics, DNS, load balancer, cache, queue [ ] Learn SOLID + 5–8 design patterns [ ] Practice 2 machine-coding/OOD problems [ ] Practice 2 system-design-lite prompts [ ] Prepare 5 STAR stories for projects/conflict/ownership/failure Eight-week balanced plan Weeks one to three Build DSA steadily and deeply enough that medium difficulty problems stop feeling unfamiliar. A good target is 90–120 problems, but quality matters more than the number. Use a structured roadmap instead of random company tags. Recent Google India and Amazon reports both reinforce that success comes from pattern mastery and articulation, not just grinding random problems. Weeks four and five Do OS, DBMS, and networking in parallel, but study them the way interviews ask them: compare/contrast, trade-offs, and production examples. Avoid spending time on low-yield theory that almost never appears in general SWE interviews. This is where most candidates can leap from “coding-only” to “well-rounded.” Week six Do OOP/OOD, design patterns, and concurrency through small designs instead of passive reading. Parking lot, Splitwise, elevator, LRU cache, and rate limiter are all useful because they force you to combine OOD, state, data structures, and thread-safety reasoning. This is especially important for product/startup flips where depth, not memorization, matters. Week seven Study system design fundamentals: availability vs consistency, caching, queues, partitioning, replication, retries, idempotency, data stores, and observability. You do not need full DDIA-level depth for most entry and junior interviews, but you do need enough to structure a design conversation. Amazon, Microsoft, Flipkart, and Google candidate evidence all show design becoming material by higher junior and mid-level roles. Week eight Run mocks and tailor to target companies: TCS/Infosys/Wipro: aptitude/pseudocode/communication plus core technical basics Amazon/Microsoft/Google: coding plus project deep dives; add design if not strictly fresher Flipkart/Swiggy/startups: coding plus machine coding/OOD/system design • • • • • • • • 33 34 35 36 • • • 11
